title: nth Roots
short: ⁿ√a is the number whose nth power is a.
trouble: Students take an even root of a negative number as if it were real.

blocks.html: In Algebra 1 you met Fractional Exponents: $x^{1/n}$ is another way to write an $n$th root. Here you look at the roots themselves, and at the one question that trips people up: when is a root a real number?

$\sqrt[n]{a}$ is the number whose $n$th power is $a$. For odd $n$ there is exactly one real $n$th root of any real number, negatives included: $\sqrt[3]{-8} = -2$. For even $n$, a negative number has no real $n$th root, and a positive number has two ($\pm$), with $\sqrt[n]{a}$ meaning the positive one.

Look at the powers. An even power is never negative: $(-3)^4 = 81$ and $3^4 = 81$. So $x^4 = 81$ has two real solutions, $x^4 = -81$ has none, and we let $\sqrt[4]{81}$ name the positive solution. An odd power keeps the sign: $(-2)^3 = -8$. Every real number is the cube (or fifth power) of exactly one real number, so odd roots always exist.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: $f(x) = x^n$ and the horizontal line $g(x) = c$. Where they meet are the real solutions of $x^n = c$. With $n$ even and $c$ negative, they never meet.

blocks.title: Odd and even roots
steps: $2^4 = 16$ (and $(-2)^4 = 16$), and the symbol means the positive root: $\sqrt[4]{16} = 2$.

blocks.title: Solving $x^n = a$
blocks.q: Find all real solutions of $x^4 = 81$, $x^3 = -27$ and $x^6 = -64$.
steps: $x^6 = -64$: even powers are never negative, so there is no real solution.

blocks.html: Taking an even root of a negative number as if it were real, for example writing $\sqrt[4]{-16} = -2$. Check by raising back: $(-2)^4 = 16$, not $-16$. No real number works, so $\sqrt[4]{-16}$ is not a real number. (Odd roots of negatives are fine.)
